metric.diagnostics.method: Compiled selected adversarial C++ programs with g++ (C++20, -Wall -Wextra, and -Wconversion) inside the sandbox and captured raw compiler diagnostic text as evidence.
metric.diagnostics.summary: C++ compiler diagnostics (GCC) are excellent for syntax errors (precise location, caret, contextual notes) but structurally weak for silent semantic hazards like integer narrowing, which require opt-in flags and remain non-fatal warnings even when enabled. No mandatory sound type/borrow checking exists at the language level (unlike Rust) to catch this class of bug at compile time by default. Score set to 58/100 reflecting strong syntactic diagnostics offset by weak default detection of a broad class of real-world numeric correctness bugs.

trials.assessment: Diagnostics are precise (line/column caret), include a helpful note pointing back to the unmatched brace, and separately flag unused-variable/statement-has-no-effect. Good syntax-error locality and secondary notes, but cascading errors from one truncation point produced two separate error messages requiring correlation by the reader.
trials.stderr_excerpt: adv22a.cpp:7:14: error: expected ';' at end of input ... adv22a.cpp:7:14: error: expected '}' at end of input ... note: to match this '{' ... warning: statement has no effect [-Wunused-value] ... warning: unused variable 'v' [-Wunused-variable]

trials.assessment: A real silent-truncation defect (implicit narrowing conversion of INT64_MAX into int32_t) is NOT diagnosed by the default warning set (-Wall -Wextra); it only surfaces with the non-default -Wconversion flag, and even then only as a warning, not an error, so the unsafe program compiles cleanly by default and misbehaves at runtime. This is a systemic weak point: C++'s implicit conversions are diagnosed opt-in rather than by default, unlike languages that reject or warn on such narrowing unconditionally.
trials.program: adversarial/ADV-01_C.cpp (int64_t -> int32_t narrowing, real correctness bug)
trials.stderr_default: (no diagnostic emitted for the narrowing conversion under -Wall -Wextra)
trials.stderr_with_flag: adv01.cpp:7:22: warning: conversion from 'int64_t' {aka 'long int'} to 'int32_t' {aka 'int'} may change value [-Wconversion]

metric.functionality_expressiveness.method: Qualitative assessment of C++20 language feature coverage exercised against the assigned adversarial/micro corpus (templates, RAII, operator overloading, constexpr, concepts, std:: containers/algorithms, exception handling, multi-paradigm support via lambdas).
observations: Corpus (template/programs/cpp/adversarial, .../micro) exercises integer overflow/narrowing (ADV-01), UB edge cases, recursion depth (ADV-21 variants), and malformed-syntax negative cases (ADV-22a/b), showing the language supports low-level numeric control needed for systems-level expressiveness.

C++ offers rich expressiveness: templates/generics with concepts, operator overloading, RAII-based resource management, multiple inheritance, lambdas/closures, coroutines (C++20), constexpr metaprogramming, and a large standard library (algorithm, ranges, containers).

Weaknesses versus more modern languages: no native sum types/pattern matching (workarounds via std::variant + std::visit are verbose), manual memory-safety discipline required (raw pointers, lifetime bugs still expressible), macro preprocessor is a blunt, non-hygienic metaprogramming tool, and template error surfaces (pre-concepts) are historically very verbose (mitigated but not eliminated by C++20 concepts).

Score reflects a mature, extremely expressive but syntactically heavy language with excellent low-level control paired with only partial adoption of modern type-safety idioms (variant/optional exist but are opt-in, not default).
metric.functionality_expressiveness.raw_score_basis: 78/100: full marks would require first-class sum types/pattern matching and eliminate macro-based metaprogramming; strong marks for generics, RAII, operator overloading, large stdlib, multi-paradigm support.
